exam1.question: In a right-dominant coronary circulation, which artery most commonly supplies the atrioventricular (AV) node?
exam1.explanation: The AV nodal artery arises from the right coronary artery in roughly 80-90% of people, which is why inferior MI is often accompanied by AV block. The circumflex supplies the AV node only in left-dominant systems.
exam1.hint: Recall where the AV nodal branch arises: near the crux of the heart, on the posterior AV groove.

exam1.question: A muscular band extending from the lower interventricular septum to the base of the anterior papillary muscle is a normal finding in which chamber?
exam1.explanation: The moderator band carries part of the right bundle branch and is a key identifier of the morphologic right ventricle. It should not be mistaken for an LV false tendon or thrombus.
exam1.hint: Think about which ventricle is defined morphologically by coarse trabeculations and a band crossing its apical cavity.

exam1.question: Which cardiac valve normally has anterior, posterior, and septal leaflets?
exam1.explanation: The tricuspid valve has three leaflets named anterior, posterior, and septal. The mitral valve has only anterior and posterior leaflets, and the semilunar valves have cusps named for coronary relationships or position.
exam1.hint: Count the leaflets and look for the one that attaches directly to the septum.

exam1.question: Isovolumic relaxation of the left ventricle begins with which event?
exam1.explanation: Isovolumic relaxation starts when the aortic valve closes and ends when LV pressure falls below LA pressure and the mitral valve opens. Mitral valve opening marks the end, not the beginning, of this phase.
exam1.hint: During this phase all valves are closed; think about which valve closes at the end of ejection.

exam1.question: On a simultaneous ECG, the mitral inflow A wave occurs immediately after which deflection?
exam1.explanation: The A wave reflects atrial contraction, which follows atrial depolarization represented by the P wave. The E wave occurs after the T wave, early in diastole.
exam1.hint: Atrial contraction follows atrial electrical activation.

exam1.question: What is the normal peak systolic pressure of the right ventricle in a healthy adult?
exam1.explanation: Normal RV systolic pressure is about 15-30 mmHg, matching pulmonary artery systolic pressure in the absence of pulmonic stenosis. Values of 100-140 mmHg are normal LV systolic pressures.
exam1.hint: The pulmonary circulation is a low-pressure, low-resistance system.

exam1.question: The first heart sound (S1) is produced mainly by closure of which valves?
exam1.explanation: S1 marks the onset of ventricular systole when the atrioventricular valves close. S2 is produced by closure of the semilunar valves at end-systole.
exam1.hint: S1 coincides with the start of ventricular systole.

exam1.question: In the parasternal long-axis view, which two aortic cusps are typically displayed?

options.text: Left coronary cusp anteriorly and right coronary cusp posteriorly
Left coronary cusp anteriorly and noncoronary cusp posteriorly
Right coronary cusp anteriorly and noncoronary cusp posteriorly
Noncoronary cusp anteriorly and left coronary cusp posteriorly

exam1.explanation: The PLAX plane typically cuts the right coronary cusp anteriorly and the noncoronary cusp posteriorly. The left coronary cusp is best seen in the parasternal short-axis view.
exam1.hint: The anterior cusp is the one nearest the RVOT and gives rise to the artery supplying the RV.

exam1.question: Which LV walls are displayed in the apical two-chamber view?
exam1.explanation: The apical two-chamber view shows the anterior and inferior walls. The four-chamber view shows the inferoseptum and anterolateral wall, and the three-chamber view shows the anteroseptum and inferolateral wall.
exam1.hint: Rotating from the four-chamber view removes the right heart and septum from the plane.

exam1.question: Which transthoracic window is used to assess inferior vena cava size and respiratory collapse?
exam1.explanation: The IVC is imaged in long axis from the subcostal window as it enters the right atrium, measured just proximal to the hepatic vein junction. The other windows do not show the intrahepatic IVC.
exam1.hint: The IVC is seen passing through the liver toward the right atrium.

exam1.question: The suprasternal notch window is primarily used to evaluate which structure?
exam1.explanation: The suprasternal view displays the ascending aorta, arch, proximal descending aorta, and the brachiocephalic, left carotid, and left subclavian origins. It is used for coarctation and dissection assessment.
exam1.hint: Think about which great vessel arches just behind the sternum's upper edge.

exam1.question: The coronary sinus drains venous blood into which chamber?
exam1.explanation: The coronary sinus runs in the posterior AV groove and empties into the right atrium near the IVC orifice, guarded by the Thebesian valve. A dilated coronary sinus suggests a persistent left SVC or elevated RA pressure.
exam1.hint: Most cardiac venous blood returns to the same chamber that receives systemic venous return.

exam1.question: In the parasternal long-axis view, a circular echo-free structure seen posterior to the left atrium, outside the pericardium, normally represents the
exam1.explanation: The descending thoracic aorta appears in cross section behind the LA in PLAX and serves as a landmark separating pericardial from pleural fluid. The coronary sinus lies within the AV groove, closer to the mitral annulus.
exam1.hint: This vessel is the landmark used to distinguish pericardial from left pleural effusion.

exam1.question: How many pulmonary veins normally enter the left atrium?
exam1.explanation: Normally four pulmonary veins (right and left upper and lower) drain into the left atrium. Variants such as a common ostium exist but the typical count is four.
exam1.hint: Each lung contributes an upper and a lower vein.

exam1.question: The anterior mitral leaflet is in direct fibrous continuity with which structure?
exam1.explanation: Aortomitral continuity links the anterior mitral leaflet to the left and noncoronary aortic cusps, which is why the anterior leaflet forms part of the LVOT. The tricuspid valve is separated from the mitral by the offset AV septum.
exam1.hint: The anterior leaflet also forms the posterior boundary of the LV outflow tract.

exam1.question: Which phase of the cardiac cycle occurs when all four valves are closed and LV pressure is rising?
exam1.explanation: Isovolumic contraction occurs between mitral valve closure and aortic valve opening, when LV pressure rises with no change in volume. Isovolumic relaxation also has all valves closed, but LV pressure is falling.
exam1.hint: Decide whether the ventricle is beginning systole or diastole.

exam1.question: What is the normal left ventricular end-diastolic pressure in a healthy adult?
exam1.explanation: Normal LVEDP is roughly 3-12 mmHg, similar to mean LA pressure. Values above about 15 mmHg indicate elevated filling pressure.
exam1.hint: LVEDP is close to mean left atrial pressure in a normal heart.

exam1.question: Using the simplified Bernoulli equation, what is the peak pressure gradient across a valve with a peak velocity of 4 m/s?
exam1.explanation: The simplified Bernoulli equation is gradient = 4V squared, so 4 x 4 squared = 64 mmHg. 16 mmHg results from forgetting the constant of 4.
exam1.hint: Square the velocity before multiplying by the constant.

exam1.question: The peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity is 3 m/s and the estimated right atrial pressure is 8 mmHg. What is the estimated RV systolic pressure?
exam1.explanation: RVSP = 4V squared + RAP = 4 x 9 + 8 = 44 mmHg. 36 mmHg omits the right atrial pressure.
exam1.hint: The TR gradient reflects the RV-to-RA difference, so the atrial pressure must be added back.

exam1.question: Per ASE guidelines, an IVC diameter of 1.8 cm that collapses more than 50% with a sniff corresponds to an estimated RA pressure of
exam1.explanation: An IVC 2.1 cm or less that collapses more than 50% indicates normal RA pressure of about 3 mmHg (0-5). A dilated IVC with less than 50% collapse suggests about 15 mmHg.
exam1.hint: A small IVC that collapses briskly indicates low right-sided filling pressure.

exam1.question: The LVOT diameter is 2.0 cm and the LVOT VTI is 20 cm. What is the stroke volume?
exam1.explanation: LVOT area = 0.785 x 2.0 squared = 3.14 square cm, and 3.14 x 20 cm = about 63 mL. 80 mL results from omitting the 0.785 (pi/4) factor.
exam1.hint: Convert the diameter to a circular area first, then multiply by the VTI.

exam1.question: A patient has a stroke volume of 70 mL and a heart rate of 80 bpm. What is the cardiac output?
exam1.explanation: Cardiac output = SV x HR = 70 mL x 80 = 5600 mL/min = 5.6 L/min. Dividing instead of multiplying gives a meaningless value near 0.9.
exam1.hint: Multiply the volume per beat by beats per minute, then convert milliliters to liters.

exam1.question: Using the continuity equation, LVOT diameter is 2.0 cm, LVOT VTI is 20 cm, and aortic valve VTI is 100 cm. What is the aortic valve area?
exam1.explanation: AVA = (LVOT area x LVOT VTI) / AV VTI = (3.14 x 20) / 100 = 0.63 square cm. 0.20 is the VTI ratio (dimensionless index), not the area.
exam1.hint: Flow through the LVOT equals flow through the valve, so solve for the unknown area.

exam1.question: Which method does the ASE recommend for calculating LV volumes and ejection fraction from 2D echocardiography?
exam1.explanation: The biplane method of disks from apical four- and two-chamber views is the recommended 2D method because it makes fewer geometric assumptions. Teichholz relies on a single linear dimension and is no longer recommended for EF.
exam1.hint: Choose the method that sums stacked slices from two orthogonal apical planes.

exam1.question: Why is the Teichholz linear method inaccurate in a patient with an apical wall motion abnormality?

options.text: It overestimates volume because it uses apical views
It requires contrast to identify the endocardium
It extrapolates volume from a basal dimension and misses regional apical dysfunction

exam1.explanation: Teichholz calculates volume from a single basal M-mode or 2D dimension, assuming uniform contraction, so an abnormal apex is not represented. Biplane disk summation accounts for regional abnormalities.
exam1.hint: Consider where the linear measurement is taken versus where the abnormality lies.

exam1.question: LV end-diastolic volume is 120 mL and end-systolic volume is 48 mL. What is the ejection fraction?
exam1.explanation: EF = (EDV - ESV) / EDV = (120 - 48) / 120 = 72/120 = 60%. 40% is the ESV/EDV ratio, not the EF.
exam1.hint: Stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume gives the fraction ejected.

exam1.question: For mitral regurgitation, the PISA radius is 1.0 cm at an aliasing velocity of 40 cm/s, and the peak MR velocity is 500 cm/s. What is the EROA?
exam1.explanation: Flow = 2 x pi x r squared x Va = 6.28 x 1 x 40 = 251 mL/s; EROA = 251 / 500 = 0.50 square cm. 0.25 results from omitting the factor of 2 in the hemisphere formula.
exam1.hint: Calculate hemispheric flow rate first, then divide by the regurgitant jet velocity.

exam1.question: Mitral inflow shows E/A 0.6 and deceleration time 260 ms, with reduced e', average E/e' of 7, and normal LA volume index. This pattern is most consistent with

options.text: Normal diastolic function in a young adult

exam1.explanation: An E/A of 0.8 or less with prolonged DT and normal filling pressure markers indicates impaired relaxation, grade I. A restrictive pattern would show E/A of 2 or more with a short DT.
exam1.hint: A dominant atrial filling wave with normal filling pressure markers points to the earliest stage.

exam1.question: Per the 2016 ASE/EACVI diastolic guideline, an average E/e' ratio greater than which value suggests elevated LV filling pressure?
exam1.explanation: An average E/e' above 14 is one of the four main criteria for elevated filling pressure. Values below 8 generally indicate normal filling pressure.
exam1.hint: The cutoff for the average ratio is lower than the old septal-only cutoff of 15.

exam1.question: What LA volume index value is considered abnormal (enlarged) in current ASE diastolic function guidelines?
exam1.explanation: An LA volume index above 34 mL/m2 is the abnormal cutoff in the 2016 guideline and reflects chronic elevation of filling pressure. 16-34 mL/m2 is the normal range.
exam1.hint: The 2016 cutoff is higher than the older 28 mL/m2 value and lower than values seen in severe LA enlargement.

exam1.question: Per the 2016 ASE/EACVI guideline, which septal e' velocity is considered abnormally reduced?
exam1.explanation: Septal e' below 7 cm/s (lateral below 10 cm/s) indicates impaired myocardial relaxation. The other values are at or above the normal septal threshold.
exam1.hint: The septal cutoff is lower than the lateral cutoff of 10 cm/s.

exam1.question: Which maneuver helps distinguish a pseudonormal mitral inflow pattern from a truly normal pattern?
exam1.explanation: Valsalva reduces preload, unmasking underlying impaired relaxation; a decrease in E/A of 50% or more supports pseudonormal filling. Leg raise increases preload and does not unmask the pattern.
exam1.hint: Lowering preload reveals the underlying relaxation abnormality.

exam1.question: According to ASE chamber quantification guidelines, LV internal dimensions in the parasternal long-axis view should be measured

options.text: At the level of the mitral leaflet tips, perpendicular to the LV long axis
At the level of the mitral annulus, parallel to the septum
At the level of the papillary muscle tips in the apical view
At the level of the aortic valve, parallel to the LVOT

exam1.explanation: ASE recommends measuring LV diameters at or just below the mitral leaflet tips, perpendicular to the long axis, at end-diastole and end-systole. Measuring at the annulus or obliquely distorts the dimension.
exam1.hint: The measurement plane is just beyond the free edge of the mitral leaflets.

exam1.question: RVOT stroke volume is 120 mL and LVOT stroke volume is 60 mL. What is the Qp:Qs ratio?
exam1.explanation: Qp:Qs = pulmonary flow / systemic flow = 120/60 = 2.0, indicating a significant left-to-right shunt. 0.5 results from inverting the ratio.
exam1.hint: Pulmonary flow goes in the numerator.

exam1.question: Which finding meets ACC/AHA criteria for severe aortic stenosis?

options.text: Aortic valve area of 1.3 square cm

exam1.explanation: Severe AS is defined by peak velocity of 4 m/s or more, mean gradient of 40 mmHg or more, or AVA under 1.0 square cm. A DVI of 0.40 and AVA of 1.3 are mild to moderate range.
exam1.hint: Recall the mean gradient threshold of severe AS.

exam1.question: The LVOT VTI is 18 cm and the aortic valve VTI is 90 cm. What does the dimensionless index indicate?
exam1.explanation: DVI = 18/90 = 0.20; a value of 0.25 or less indicates severe AS. The DVI avoids LVOT diameter measurement error.
exam1.hint: Divide the LVOT VTI by the valve VTI and compare with the 0.25 cutoff.

exam1.question: What is the most common cause of aortic stenosis in patients older than 70 years in developed countries?

options.text: Degenerative calcific disease of a trileaflet valve

exam1.explanation: Age-related calcific degeneration of a trileaflet valve dominates in the elderly. Bicuspid valves are the leading cause in younger adults, and rheumatic AS almost always coexists with mitral disease.
exam1.hint: Think of the age-related process that starts as sclerosis.

exam1.question: On parasternal short-axis imaging, a bicuspid aortic valve classically shows

options.text: A 'Mercedes-Benz' sign in diastole with three equal cusps
Diastolic doming of the anterior leaflet

exam1.explanation: A bicuspid valve opens with an elliptical fish-mouth orifice in systole, and a raphe may make it look trileaflet in diastole. The Mercedes-Benz sign describes a normal trileaflet valve, so systolic imaging is essential.
exam1.hint: Assess the valve in systole, because a raphe can mislead in diastole.

exam1.question: A bicuspid aortic valve is most commonly associated with which other abnormality?
exam1.explanation: Bicuspid aortic valve is associated with coarctation and with aortopathy of the ascending aorta; when coarctation is found, a bicuspid valve is present in a large proportion of patients. Ebstein anomaly involves the tricuspid valve.
exam1.hint: The associated lesion is a narrowing of the aorta near the ligamentum arteriosum.

exam1.question: In the parasternal long-axis view, rheumatic mitral stenosis classically shows

options.text: Systolic anterior motion of the anterior leaflet
Posterior leaflet bowing beyond the annulus in systole
Diastolic doming of the anterior leaflet with a 'hockey stick' appearance

exam1.explanation: Commissural fusion restricts the leaflet tips so the body of the anterior leaflet domes in diastole, producing the hockey stick shape. SAM is a feature of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.
exam1.hint: Fused commissures tether the tips while the leaflet body still moves.

exam1.question: The mitral pressure half-time is 220 ms. What is the estimated mitral valve area?
exam1.explanation: MVA = 220 / PHT = 220 / 220 = 1.0 square cm. A longer pressure half-time indicates a smaller orifice.
exam1.hint: Recall the empiric constant in the Hatle pressure half-time formula and divide it by the measured PHT.

exam1.question: Per current ACC/AHA guidelines, severe rheumatic mitral stenosis is defined by a mitral valve area of
exam1.explanation: Severe MS is MVA 1.5 square cm or less (very severe 1.0 or less), usually with a mean gradient above 5-10 mmHg at normal heart rates. Normal MVA is 4-6 square cm.
exam1.hint: This threshold is higher than the severe aortic valve area cutoff.

exam1.question: Mitral valve area planimetry should be performed in the parasternal short-axis view at which level?
exam1.explanation: The stenotic funnel's smallest orifice is at the leaflet tips, so planimetry is done there in mid-diastole. Scanning at the annulus or body overestimates area.
exam1.hint: Sweep from base toward apex until the smallest orifice is found.

exam1.question: Why does significant aortic regurgitation make the pressure half-time method unreliable in mitral stenosis?

options.text: It lengthens PHT and underestimates valve area
It causes aliasing of the mitral CW signal
It raises LV diastolic pressure rapidly, shortening PHT and overestimating valve area
It reduces LA pressure and abolishes the gradient

exam1.explanation: Regurgitant aortic flow fills the LV from a second source, so the LA-LV gradient falls faster and PHT shortens, overestimating MVA. Reduced LV compliance and recent valvotomy also invalidate PHT.
exam1.hint: Think about what extra diastolic LV filling does to how quickly the transmitral gradient decays.

exam1.question: Which complication is most closely associated with significant rheumatic mitral stenosis?

options.text: Right ventricular hypertrophy with septal bounce

exam1.explanation: MS causes LA enlargement, stasis, spontaneous echo contrast, and atrial fibrillation, all predisposing to LA appendage thrombus. LV apical thrombus is typical of anterior MI with apical akinesis.
exam1.hint: Stasis occurs in the chamber upstream of the stenosis.

exam1.question: Why should heart rate be reported with a mean transmitral gradient in mitral stenosis?

options.text: Heart rate alters the planimetered area
Tachycardia shortens diastole and raises the gradient
Tachycardia lowers the gradient by reducing flow time

exam1.explanation: The mean gradient depends on flow and diastolic filling time; faster heart rates shorten diastole and increase the gradient for the same valve area. Planimetry is relatively independent of heart rate.
exam1.hint: The gradient is flow and time dependent; area by planimetry is not.

exam1.question: Which peak velocity across the pulmonic valve indicates severe pulmonic stenosis?
exam1.explanation: Severe PS is defined by peak velocity above 4 m/s (peak gradient above 64 mmHg). Normal pulmonic velocity is under about 1 m/s.
exam1.hint: The severe velocity cutoff is the same one used for severe aortic stenosis.

exam1.question: Carcinoid heart disease most characteristically affects which valves?
exam1.explanation: Vasoactive substances from hepatic metastases reach the right heart before lung inactivation, causing thickened, retracted, fixed tricuspid and pulmonic leaflets. Left-sided involvement suggests a right-to-left shunt or lung primary.
exam1.hint: Consider where hepatic metastases release vasoactive substances and which valves they reach first.

exam1.question: The most common cause of tricuspid stenosis in adults is

options.text: Rheumatic disease, usually with mitral involvement

exam1.explanation: Rheumatic heart disease is the leading cause of tricuspid stenosis and almost always coexists with mitral valve disease. Carcinoid is a less common cause; Ebstein typically causes regurgitation.
exam1.hint: Tricuspid stenosis in adults is usually acquired and rarely occurs as an isolated lesion.

exam1.question: A patient with LVEF 30% has an AVA of 0.8 square cm and a mean gradient of 25 mmHg. Which test best distinguishes true severe from pseudosevere aortic stenosis?
exam1.explanation: In low-flow, low-gradient AS with reduced EF, low-dose dobutamine increases flow: true severe AS shows a rising gradient with AVA staying under 1.0, while pseudosevere AS shows the area increasing. It also assesses contractile reserve.
exam1.hint: Increase flow pharmacologically and watch whether the valve area or the gradient changes.

exam1.question: To avoid underestimating aortic stenosis severity, CW Doppler interrogation should include which window in addition to apical?

options.text: Parasternal short axis at the papillary level

exam1.explanation: The highest AS velocity may be obtained from the right parasternal or suprasternal windows, often with a dedicated nonimaging probe. Relying only on the apical window risks a nonparallel intercept angle.
exam1.hint: The jet direction may be better aligned from a window to the right of the sternum.

exam1.question: Which vena contracta width indicates severe mitral regurgitation?
exam1.explanation: A vena contracta of 0.7 cm or more indicates severe MR, and under 0.3 cm indicates mild. Values in between are intermediate and need other parameters.
exam1.hint: The severe MR threshold is slightly larger than the AR threshold.

exam1.question: Which vena contracta width indicates severe aortic regurgitation?
exam1.explanation: An AR vena contracta above 0.6 cm is severe and under 0.3 cm is mild. It is measured in PLAX at the narrowest neck of the jet.
exam1.hint: This threshold is about 0.1 cm smaller than the MR threshold.

exam1.question: Which aortic regurgitation pressure half-time indicates severe AR?
exam1.explanation: Severe AR causes rapid equalization of aortic and LV diastolic pressures, giving a PHT under 200 ms; over 500 ms suggests mild AR. PHT is also shortened by elevated LV diastolic pressure from other causes.
exam1.hint: Faster pressure equalization means a steeper slope and shorter time.

exam1.question: Holodiastolic flow reversal in the proximal abdominal aorta is a specific sign of
exam1.explanation: Holodiastolic reversal in the descending thoracic and especially the abdominal aorta indicates severe AR. Brief early diastolic reversal can be normal.
exam1.hint: Retrograde diastolic flow far down the aorta implies a large regurgitant volume back into the LV.

exam1.question: Systolic flow reversal in the pulmonary veins is a specific sign of
exam1.explanation: A large MR jet raises LA pressure in systole enough to reverse pulmonary venous S-wave flow. Blunted S waves are less specific and also occur with AF and elevated LA pressure.
exam1.hint: Ask which lesion pushes blood back into the left atrium during systole.

exam1.question: For primary (degenerative) mitral regurgitation, which EROA indicates severe MR?
exam1.explanation: An EROA of 0.40 square cm or more with regurgitant volume of 60 mL or more defines severe primary MR. Under 0.20 square cm is mild.
exam1.hint: The severe EROA threshold is twice the mild upper limit.

exam1.question: Systolic flow reversal in the hepatic veins most strongly suggests
exam1.explanation: In severe TR, the regurgitant jet transmits RA systolic pressure to the hepatic veins, reversing systolic flow. Expiratory diastolic reversal is the hepatic vein pattern of constriction.
exam1.hint: Note the timing of the reversal in the cardiac cycle.

exam1.question: Mitral valve prolapse is diagnosed when a leaflet is displaced beyond the mitral annular plane in systole by more than

options.text: 2 mm in the parasternal long-axis view
2 mm in the apical four-chamber view
5 mm in the apical two-chamber view

exam1.explanation: MVP requires systolic displacement over 2 mm above the annular plane in PLAX. The saddle-shaped annulus makes leaflets appear to prolapse in the apical four-chamber view, causing false positives.
exam1.hint: The saddle shape of the annulus makes some views unreliable for this diagnosis.

exam1.question: A flail posterior mitral leaflet typically produces an MR jet that is directed

options.text: Anteriorly, away from the flail leaflet

exam1.explanation: In a primary leaflet lesion, the jet is directed away from the abnormal leaflet, so a posterior flail produces an anteriorly directed jet hugging the atrial septum. Restricted leaflets (Carpentier IIIb) direct jets toward the affected side.
exam1.hint: With excess leaflet motion, the jet is deflected by the opposite, normal leaflet.

exam1.question: Valvular vegetations from infective endocarditis are most commonly attached to the

options.text: Downstream side, such as the aortic side of the aortic cusps
Upstream (low-pressure) side of the valve, such as the atrial side of the mitral leaflets

exam1.explanation: Vegetations typically form on the low-pressure side of the jet: the atrial side of AV valves and the ventricular side of semilunar valves. They are mobile, irregular, and move independently of the leaflet.
exam1.hint: Think about which surface faces the incoming regurgitant jet.

exam1.question: An echolucent or echodense thickening in the aortic root wall adjacent to an infected aortic valve most likely represents
exam1.explanation: Root abscess is a serious complication of aortic valve endocarditis and appears as perivalvular thickening or an echolucent cavity; TEE is far more sensitive than TTE. Lambl excrescences are thin strands on the cusp closure line.
exam1.hint: Consider how infection extends beyond the leaflets into adjacent tissue.

exam1.question: In a bileaflet mechanical mitral prosthesis, several small, brief, symmetric regurgitant jets within the sewing ring most likely represent
exam1.explanation: Mechanical valves have built-in small washing jets inside the ring to reduce thrombus formation; they are short, low-momentum, and symmetric. Paravalvular leaks arise outside the sewing ring.
exam1.hint: Note where the jets originate relative to the sewing ring and how they look.

exam1.question: Abnormal rocking motion of a prosthetic valve sewing ring is most suggestive of
exam1.explanation: Rocking of the sewing ring indicates partial detachment (dehiscence), usually with a large paravalvular leak, and is a surgical problem. A well-seated ring moves with the annulus without independent motion.
exam1.hint: A securely sutured ring should not move independently of the annulus.

exam1.question: A regurgitant jet that originates outside the sewing ring of a prosthetic valve is classified as
exam1.explanation: Jets arising between the sewing ring and the native annulus are paravalvular leaks, which are pathologic. Transvalvular jets pass through the valve itself.
exam1.hint: Classify the jet by its origin relative to the ring.

exam1.question: Why is TEE preferred over TTE for evaluating suspected regurgitation of a mechanical mitral prosthesis?

options.text: On TTE, acoustic shadowing from the prosthesis obscures the left atrium

exam1.explanation: From the apex, the prosthesis shadows the LA so MR jets are hidden; TEE images from behind the LA and avoids the shadow. TTE can still measure mitral gradients well.
exam1.hint: Consider which side of the prosthesis the transducer views from each approach.

exam1.question: Which finding suggests obstruction of a prosthetic aortic valve?
exam1.explanation: A DVI below 0.25 with a rounded contour and acceleration time over 100 ms suggests prosthetic AV obstruction. A normal prosthesis typically has a DVI of 0.30 or more and an early-peaking, triangular contour.
exam1.hint: Compare the LVOT-to-valve velocity ratio with the 0.25 cutoff.

exam1.question: A dense pulmonic regurgitation CW signal with a steep deceleration and pressure half-time under 100 ms that ends before end-diastole indicates
exam1.explanation: Severe PR causes rapid equalization of PA and RV diastolic pressures, so the signal is dense with a short PHT and may terminate early. Pulmonary hypertension produces a high-velocity PR jet with a slow decline.
exam1.hint: Rapid pressure equalization between two chambers indicates a large regurgitant orifice.

exam1.question: An increased E-point septal separation (EPSS) greater than 7 mm on M-mode most commonly indicates
exam1.explanation: EPSS increases when a dilated, poorly contracting LV receives low mitral flow, so leaflets open less toward the septum; over 7 mm suggests reduced EF. Mitral stenosis and AR can also increase EPSS, which is why it is a supportive sign.
exam1.hint: The measurement reflects how far the anterior leaflet opens toward the septum in early diastole.

exam1.question: In an adult without another cause of hypertrophy, which maximal LV wall thickness meets the usual diagnostic threshold for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
exam1.explanation: A maximal wall thickness of 15 mm or more in any segment, unexplained by loading conditions, is the standard HCM threshold (13 mm with a positive family history). 30 mm or more is a sudden death risk marker.
exam1.hint: The threshold is clearly above the upper limit of normal wall thickness (about 10-11 mm) but well below the extreme values used for sudden-death risk.

exam1.question: In obstructive HCM with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, the associated MR jet is typically directed
exam1.explanation: SAM pulls the anterior leaflet into the LVOT and opens a gap, sending the MR jet posteriorly. An anteriorly directed jet with SAM should raise suspicion of intrinsic mitral leaflet disease.
exam1.hint: The anterior leaflet is pulled away from coaptation, so the jet leaves in the opposite direction.

exam1.question: The CW Doppler signal from dynamic LVOT obstruction in HCM typically appears
exam1.explanation: Dynamic obstruction worsens as the LV empties, so velocity peaks late in systole giving a dagger shape. Fixed valvular AS produces a more rounded, earlier-peaking envelope.
exam1.hint: Dynamic obstruction increases as the cavity gets smaller through systole.

exam1.question: Which maneuver increases the LVOT gradient in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy?
exam1.explanation: Valsalva strain decreases preload, making the LV cavity smaller and worsening obstruction. Squatting, leg raise, and handgrip increase preload or afterload and reduce the gradient.
exam1.hint: Anything that shrinks the LV cavity worsens dynamic obstruction.

exam1.question: In hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, M-mode of the aortic valve characteristically shows

options.text: Mid-systolic partial closure (notching) of the aortic cusps
Diastolic fluttering of the anterior mitral leaflet
Early systolic closure of the mitral valve

exam1.explanation: Dynamic LVOT obstruction abruptly reduces flow in mid-systole, causing partial closure of the aortic cusps, then reopening. Diastolic fluttering of the anterior mitral leaflet is a sign of AR.
exam1.hint: Flow through the valve drops abruptly halfway through ejection.

exam1.question: Hypertrophy confined to the LV apex, giving a 'spade-shaped' cavity in diastole and giant T-wave inversions, describes
exam1.explanation: Apical HCM (Yamaguchi variant) produces a spade-shaped cavity and deep precordial T-wave inversions; contrast helps define apical thickness. Thrombus usually occurs in an akinetic, not hypertrophied, apex.
exam1.hint: The cavity shape results from thickened walls near the tip.

exam1.question: A global longitudinal strain bull's-eye map showing markedly reduced basal and mid strain with relatively preserved apical strain is most suggestive of
exam1.explanation: Apical sparing (a cherry-on-top pattern) is characteristic of cardiac amyloidosis, along with thick walls, granular sparkling, biatrial enlargement, and low ECG voltage. LAD infarction reduces apical strain.
exam1.hint: The pattern spares the region that is typically involved first in coronary disease of the LAD.

exam1.question: Which mitral inflow pattern is characteristic of advanced restrictive cardiomyopathy?

options.text: E/A less than 0.8 with deceleration time over 240 ms
E/A of 1.2 with normal deceleration time
Absent E wave with a single A wave
E/A greater than 2 with deceleration time under 160 ms

exam1.explanation: High LA pressure produces a tall E wave that decelerates quickly because the stiff LV equalizes pressure rapidly. E/A under 0.8 with prolonged DT is impaired relaxation.
exam1.hint: A stiff ventricle fills early and abruptly.

exam1.question: In left ventricular noncompaction, which finding supports the diagnosis on short-axis imaging?

options.text: A single trabeculation near the apex
Dyskinetic apex with a wide neck
Noncompacted-to-compacted myocardial thickness ratio greater than 2 in end-systole

exam1.explanation: LVNC shows prominent trabeculations with deep recesses filled with blood on color Doppler, and a noncompacted to compacted ratio over 2.0 in systole (Jenni criteria). A few apical trabeculations are normal.
exam1.hint: The criterion compares two myocardial layers at end-systole.

exam1.question: A postmenopausal woman with chest pain after emotional stress has apical and mid-LV akinesis with hyperkinetic basal segments, extending beyond a single coronary territory. The most likely diagnosis is

options.text: Acute LAD occlusion with ventricular septal rupture

exam1.explanation: Takotsubo classically shows apical ballooning with hyperdynamic base, wall motion abnormalities crossing coronary territories, and recovery within weeks. LAD occlusion generally respects one coronary distribution.
exam1.hint: Note that the dysfunction does not match one artery's territory.

exam1.question: Per ASE guidelines, which TAPSE value indicates RV systolic dysfunction?
exam1.explanation: TAPSE under 17 mm is abnormal per ASE 2015 chamber quantification. It is an M-mode measure of longitudinal tricuspid annular motion in the apical four-chamber view.
exam1.hint: A normal TAPSE is roughly 2-2.5 cm; the abnormal cutoff is below the lower end of that range.

exam1.question: A tissue Doppler RV S' velocity less than which value indicates RV systolic dysfunction?
exam1.explanation: An RV S' under 9.5 cm/s at the lateral tricuspid annulus indicates reduced RV longitudinal function per ASE 2015. It is angle-dependent and requires alignment with the free wall.
exam1.hint: RV S' is a low-velocity tissue Doppler signal; the cutoff is in single digits but well above very severe dysfunction values.

exam1.question: What RV fractional area change (FAC) indicates RV systolic dysfunction?
exam1.explanation: FAC under 35% is abnormal per ASE 2015 and is calculated from RV end-diastolic and end-systolic areas in an RV-focused apical view. Values of 55-60% are in the range of LVEF thresholds (ASE 2015 normal LVEF about 52% or more in men, 54% or more in women), not RV FAC.
exam1.hint: The RV normal threshold is lower than that for LVEF.

exam1.question: In the parasternal short-axis view, flattening of the interventricular septum predominantly during systole indicates
exam1.explanation: Systolic septal flattening (D-shaped LV) occurs when RV systolic pressure approaches LV pressure, as in pulmonary hypertension. Diastolic-predominant flattening indicates RV volume overload, as in an ASD.
exam1.hint: Match the timing of septal flattening to the type of RV load.

exam1.question: RV free wall akinesis with preserved apical contraction in a patient with acute dyspnea is known as McConnell sign and suggests
exam1.explanation: McConnell sign is a classic, fairly specific finding of acute PE with sudden RV pressure overload. Chronic pulmonary hypertension typically shows RV hypertrophy with global dysfunction.
exam1.hint: The sign reflects sudden pressure loading of a previously normal RV.

exam1.question: A pulmonary artery (RVOT) acceleration time shorter than about 100 ms, especially with mid-systolic notching, suggests
exam1.explanation: Elevated pulmonary vascular resistance causes rapid early acceleration and a short AT, often with mid-systolic notching. A normal PA flow profile has a rounded, later peak with AT usually over 130 ms.
exam1.hint: Higher pulmonary vascular resistance makes flow peak earlier.

exam1.question: How many segments are in the ASE-recommended LV segmentation model that includes the apical cap?
exam1.explanation: The 17-segment model adds the apical cap to the 16-segment model and is recommended for myocardial perfusion and wall motion assessment. 18 segments is an older apical scheme.
exam1.hint: Basal and mid levels have six segments each, the apex four, plus one more.

exam1.question: Using the ASE wall motion scoring system, a dyskinetic segment receives a score of
exam1.explanation: ASE scoring is 1 normal or hyperkinetic, 2 hypokinetic, 3 akinetic, and 4 dyskinetic. Akinesis (no thickening) scores 3; dyskinesis (outward systolic motion) is worse.
exam1.hint: Higher scores represent progressively worse wall motion, and outward motion is the worst category.

exam1.question: What is the wall motion score index of a normal left ventricle?
exam1.explanation: WMSI is the sum of segment scores divided by the number of segments scored; all normal segments give 1.0. Higher values indicate more extensive dysfunction.
exam1.hint: Divide the total score by the number of segments when every segment is normal.

exam1.question: The left anterior descending artery typically supplies which LV regions?

options.text: Anterior wall, anterior septum, and apex
RV free wall and inferior wall

exam1.explanation: The LAD supplies the anterior wall, anteroseptum, and most of the apex. The inferior wall and basal inferoseptum are usually RCA territory.
exam1.hint: The artery runs in the anterior interventricular groove toward the apex.

exam1.question: Which territory is most typically supplied by the right coronary artery in a right-dominant system?

options.text: Inferior wall, basal inferoseptum, and RV free wall

exam1.explanation: The RCA supplies the RV, the inferior wall, and the basal inferoseptum through the PDA. Inferior MI should prompt assessment for RV involvement.
exam1.hint: The PDA travels in the posterior interventricular groove.

exam1.question: The left circumflex artery most typically supplies which LV walls?

options.text: Inferior wall and RV free wall

exam1.explanation: The circumflex runs in the left AV groove and supplies the lateral walls through obtuse marginal branches. Overlap with RCA and LAD varies with dominance.
exam1.hint: Its branches are called obtuse marginals and reach the side of the LV.

exam1.question: A post-infarction LV outpouching with a wide neck, a wall composed of thinned myocardium, and dyskinesis, most often at the apex, is a
exam1.explanation: A true aneurysm involves all wall layers with a wide neck and is most often apical after LAD infarction. A pseudoaneurysm has a narrow neck and is a contained rupture.
exam1.hint: Compare the neck width with the maximal diameter of the cavity.

exam1.question: Which feature best distinguishes an LV pseudoaneurysm from a true aneurysm?

options.text: Narrow neck with a neck-to-maximal-diameter ratio under 0.5

exam1.explanation: A pseudoaneurysm is a free-wall rupture contained by pericardium, with an abrupt narrow neck (ratio under 0.5), often inferior or inferolateral. True aneurysms have wide necks; both can contain thrombus.
exam1.hint: Think about how a contained rupture connects to the cavity.

exam1.question: A patient several days after an anterior MI develops a new holosystolic murmur, and color Doppler shows systolic flow across the apical septum from LV to RV. This is
exam1.explanation: Septal rupture after anterior MI typically involves the apical septum and shows left-to-right flow across the defect. Papillary muscle rupture also causes a new murmur but with severe MR into the LA.
exam1.hint: Follow where the abnormal systolic jet travels.

exam1.question: Which papillary muscle most commonly ruptures after acute myocardial infarction?

options.text: Anterolateral, because it has a dual blood supply
Septal papillary muscle of the tricuspid valve
Posteromedial, because it usually has a single blood supply

exam1.explanation: The posteromedial papillary muscle is usually supplied only by the PDA, so inferior MI can infarct it; it ruptures several times more often. The anterolateral muscle has dual LAD and circumflex supply.
exam1.hint: Vulnerability relates to how many arteries supply each muscle.

exam1.question: Following an anterior MI, LV thrombus is most likely found

options.text: At an akinetic or dyskinetic apex

exam1.explanation: Apical thrombus forms where blood stagnates in an akinetic or aneurysmal apex after LAD infarction. Ultrasound enhancing agents improve detection when the apex is poorly seen.
exam1.hint: Thrombus forms where flow stagnates beside a noncontracting wall.

exam1.question: During dobutamine stress, a hypokinetic segment that improves at low dose and then worsens at high dose (biphasic response) indicates
exam1.explanation: The biphasic response is the most specific sign of hibernating, viable myocardium supplied by a stenotic artery, predicting recovery after revascularization. Scar shows no improvement at any dose.
exam1.hint: Low dose tests contractile reserve; high dose tests flow reserve.

exam1.question: Which finding constitutes a positive stress echocardiogram for ischemia?

options.text: A new or worsening wall motion abnormality with stress
Hyperdynamic wall motion at peak stress
Decrease in LV cavity size at peak stress
Mild increase in heart rate above baseline

exam1.explanation: Ischemia is indicated by a new or worsening regional wall motion abnormality, often with LV cavity dilation. Normal response is hyperkinesis with a smaller cavity.
exam1.hint: Compare regional function at rest versus peak stress.

exam1.question: What is the target heart rate for a 60-year-old patient undergoing stress echocardiography?
exam1.explanation: Target heart rate is 85% of the age-predicted maximum (220 - age): 0.85 x 160 = 136 bpm. 160 bpm is the maximum, not the target.
exam1.hint: Start with 220 minus age, then take 85% of it.

exam1.question: In treadmill exercise stress echocardiography, post-exercise images should be acquired

options.text: After the heart rate returns to baseline
Within about 1 minute of stopping exercise

exam1.explanation: Wall motion abnormalities can resolve quickly after exercise, so images are acquired as soon as possible, ideally within 60-90 seconds. Waiting for HR recovery reduces sensitivity.
exam1.hint: Ischemic wall motion abnormalities fade quickly with recovery.

exam1.question: During dobutamine stress echocardiography, which medication is commonly added when target heart rate is not reached?
exam1.explanation: Atropine blocks vagal tone and helps achieve target heart rate. Esmolol (a beta-blocker) is used to reverse dobutamine effects, not to augment heart rate.
exam1.hint: The agent works by blocking vagal (parasympathetic) slowing of the sinus node.

exam1.question: A thin (end-diastolic thickness under 6 mm), echogenic, akinetic segment in the territory of a prior infarct most likely represents
exam1.explanation: Chronic transmural infarction causes wall thinning and increased echogenicity from fibrosis, indicating nonviability. Hibernating myocardium usually has preserved wall thickness.
exam1.hint: Fibrosis replaces muscle and the wall thins over time.

exam1.question: In the parasternal long-axis view, which finding indicates that posterior fluid is pericardial rather than left pleural?

options.text: Fluid extends posterior to the descending thoracic aorta
Fluid is seen only lateral to the left atrium
Fluid tapers anterior to the descending thoracic aorta

exam1.explanation: Pericardial effusion lies anterior to the descending aorta, between it and the LA, while pleural fluid extends posterior and lateral to the aorta. A floating lung segment is a pleural finding.
exam1.hint: Use the descending aorta as the landmark.

exam1.question: Which echo finding of cardiac tamponade involves the right atrium?

options.text: Systolic collapse (inversion) lasting more than one-third of the cardiac cycle
Systolic flow reversal in the RA appendage
Persistent RA enlargement with a thickened wall

exam1.explanation: RA collapse during late diastole and systole occurs early in tamponade, and inversion lasting over one-third of the cycle is highly specific. RV diastolic collapse is less sensitive but more specific overall.
exam1.hint: The thin-walled RA is compressed when its pressure is lowest.

exam1.question: In cardiac tamponade, mitral inflow Doppler typically shows

options.text: An inspiratory decrease in E velocity greater than about 25-30%
An inspiratory increase in E velocity greater than 25%
E/A ratio greater than 2 with no variation

exam1.explanation: Ventricular interdependence in tamponade causes exaggerated inspiratory decrease of mitral E (over about 25-30%) and increase of tricuspid E. Normal variation is under about 10-15%.
exam1.hint: During inspiration, right heart filling increases at the expense of the left.

exam1.question: In cardiac tamponade, the inferior vena cava typically appears

options.text: Dilated with less than 50% inspiratory collapse (plethora)
Normal size with more than 50% collapse

exam1.explanation: Elevated RA pressure causes IVC plethora, which is a sensitive but nonspecific tamponade sign. A collapsing IVC makes tamponade unlikely except in hypovolemia.
exam1.hint: Tamponade raises right atrial pressure.

exam1.question: Which hepatic vein Doppler finding is characteristic of constrictive pericarditis?

options.text: Prominent diastolic flow reversal during expiration

exam1.explanation: In constriction, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein reversal reflects ventricular interdependence. Restrictive cardiomyopathy shows inspiratory reversal, and severe TR causes systolic reversal.
exam1.hint: Constriction and restriction differ in the respiratory phase of reversal.

exam1.question: In constrictive pericarditis, mitral annular tissue Doppler typically shows

options.text: Medial e' equal to or greater than lateral e' (annulus reversus)
Lateral e' much greater than medial e'
Markedly reduced medial and lateral e' below 5 cm/s

exam1.explanation: In constriction, lateral motion is tethered by the pericardium, so medial e' is often equal to or higher than lateral (annulus reversus), and medial e' is preserved. Restrictive cardiomyopathy shows reduced e'.
exam1.hint: Consider which annular site is tethered by the stiff pericardium.

exam1.question: An anterior echo-free or speckled space seen only anterior to the RV, without a posterior component, most likely represents
exam1.explanation: An isolated anterior space, often granular and moving with the heart, is usually epicardial fat; small effusions accumulate posteriorly first in the supine patient. Fat is common in older and obese patients.
exam1.hint: Consider where free fluid collects first in a supine patient.

exam1.question: A mobile, gelatinous left atrial mass attached by a stalk to the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis is most likely a
exam1.explanation: Myxoma is the most common primary benign cardiac tumor in adults, typically in the LA attached to the fossa ovalis region, and may prolapse into the LV in diastole. Fibroelastomas are small and valvular.
exam1.hint: The stalk attachment site is a classic clue.

exam1.question: A small, mobile, frond-like mass on the aortic valve in an older adult is most likely
exam1.explanation: Papillary fibroelastoma is the most common primary valvular tumor, usually on the aortic valve, with a frond-like 'sea anemone' appearance; it carries embolic risk. Vegetations are the main differential.
exam1.hint: The most common valvular tumor has a sea anemone shape.

exam1.question: What is the most common tumor involving the heart in adults?
exam1.explanation: Secondary tumors (lung, breast, melanoma, lymphoma) are far more common than primary cardiac tumors, often involving the pericardium. Myxoma is the most common primary tumor.
exam1.hint: Primary cardiac tumors are rare compared with spread from elsewhere.

exam1.question: A highly mobile, filamentous, net-like structure in the right atrium near the IVC and coronary sinus orifices is most likely
exam1.explanation: A Chiari network is a remnant of the right sinus venosus valve and appears as a fenestrated, highly mobile structure. A Eustachian valve is a more fixed ridge at the IVC-RA junction.
exam1.hint: Contrast a fenestrated, waving remnant with a fixed ridge.

exam1.question: A linear, ridge-like structure at the junction of the IVC and right atrium, seen in the RV inflow or subcostal view, is most likely
exam1.explanation: The Eustachian valve is an embryologic remnant guarding the IVC orifice and is a normal variant. It can direct flow toward the atrial septum and should not be confused with thrombus.
exam1.hint: Name the remnant that once directed IVC flow toward the foramen ovale.

exam1.question: On TEE, a left atrial appendage emptying velocity less than which value is associated with increased thrombus risk?
exam1.explanation: LAA emptying velocity under 20 cm/s indicates stasis and higher thrombus and stroke risk, often with spontaneous echo contrast. Normal velocities are usually above 40 cm/s.
exam1.hint: Low velocity means stasis; the cutoff is a low two-digit number.

exam1.question: A dumbbell-shaped thickening of the interatrial septum that spares the fossa ovalis is characteristic of

options.text: Lipomatous hypertrophy of the interatrial septum

exam1.explanation: Lipomatous hypertrophy is benign fat deposition that spares the thin fossa ovalis, producing a dumbbell shape. Myxoma typically arises from the fossa ovalis region, the area spared here.
exam1.hint: The thin central portion of the septum is not involved.

exam1.question: On TEE, a prominent tissue fold between the left atrial appendage and the left upper pulmonary vein that may mimic thrombus is the
exam1.explanation: The ridge between the LAA and left upper pulmonary vein is a normal structure that can have a bulbous tip and be mistaken for thrombus. The crista terminalis is in the right atrium.
exam1.hint: This normal left atrial structure lies in the left lateral atrial wall, between the appendage orifice and a pulmonary vein.

exam1.question: A swinging heart within a large pericardial effusion corresponds to which ECG finding?
exam1.explanation: Beat-to-beat swinging of the heart changes the QRS axis and amplitude, producing electrical alternans, a classic sign of large effusion and tamponade. Delta waves indicate pre-excitation.
exam1.hint: The QRS amplitude changes with each beat as the heart's position shifts.

exam1.question: What is the most common type of atrial septal defect in adults?
exam1.explanation: Secundum ASDs at the fossa ovalis account for about 70-75% of ASDs. Primum defects are part of the AV canal spectrum.
exam1.hint: The most common defect involves the central fossa ovalis region.

exam1.question: A superior sinus venosus ASD is most commonly associated with

options.text: Partial anomalous drainage of the right upper pulmonary vein

exam1.explanation: Superior sinus venosus defects sit near the SVC-RA junction and usually coexist with anomalous right upper pulmonary venous return. TEE bicaval views help identify them.
exam1.hint: The defect lies near the SVC, close to where the right upper lung drains.

exam1.question: A primum atrial septal defect is commonly associated with
exam1.explanation: Primum ASD is a partial AV septal defect and often has a cleft anterior mitral leaflet with MR. Anomalous pulmonary venous return pairs with sinus venosus defects.
exam1.hint: This defect is part of the AV canal spectrum, affecting the AV valves.

exam1.question: Which ventricular septal defect type is most common?
exam1.explanation: Perimembranous VSDs are the most common type, located just below the aortic valve near the septal tricuspid leaflet. Muscular defects are common in infants and often close spontaneously.
exam1.hint: The most common defect lies near the tricuspid septal leaflet and below the aortic valve.

exam1.question: A hemodynamically significant secundum ASD most typically causes

options.text: RV and RA dilation with diastolic septal flattening
Systolic septal flattening from LV pressure overload
LA and LV dilation without right heart changes

exam1.explanation: Left-to-right atrial shunting volume-loads the right heart, causing RA and RV enlargement and diastolic septal flattening (paradoxical septal motion). Systolic flattening suggests pressure overload.
exam1.hint: Atrial-level shunts overload the chambers that receive the extra flow.

exam1.question: A patent ductus arteriosus in an adult classically shows continuous flow into which structure?

options.text: Right atrium near the coronary sinus
Ascending aorta above the sinotubular junction
Main pulmonary artery near the left pulmonary artery origin

exam1.explanation: A PDA connects the proximal descending aorta (beyond the left subclavian) to the PA near the left pulmonary artery, producing continuous flow into the PA in the PSAX view. The aortic pressure exceeds PA pressure in both phases.
exam1.hint: The ductus connects the descending aorta to the pulmonary trunk bifurcation.

exam1.question: On CW Doppler of the descending aorta from the suprasternal window, significant coarctation characteristically shows

options.text: Low systolic velocity with holodiastolic flow reversal
Normal velocity with no diastolic flow
High systolic velocity with persistent antegrade diastolic flow (diastolic tail)
Biphasic low-velocity flow with early diastolic reversal

exam1.explanation: A significant coarctation produces a high systolic velocity and a persistent diastolic gradient, giving a sawtooth diastolic tail. Holodiastolic reversal is the sign of severe AR.
exam1.hint: A fixed narrowing maintains a pressure gradient even in diastole.

exam1.question: Ebstein anomaly is diagnosed when the septal tricuspid leaflet is apically displaced relative to the mitral leaflet by
exam1.explanation: Normal tricuspid offset is small; an apical displacement of 8 mm/m2 or more in the four-chamber view indicates Ebstein anomaly with an atrialized RV. Some offset is normal and expected.
exam1.hint: Normal apical offset of the tricuspid valve exists, so the abnormal threshold is indexed and larger.

exam1.question: Which conduction abnormality is classically associated with Ebstein anomaly?
exam1.explanation: Ebstein anomaly is associated with accessory pathways (WPW) and supraventricular tachycardia, and often with a PFO or secundum ASD. Congenital complete heart block is associated with corrected transposition.
exam1.hint: The displaced tricuspid annulus disrupts the normal electrical insulation between the atria and ventricles.

exam1.question: What is the most common long-term residual lesion after tetralogy of Fallot repair with a transannular patch?
exam1.explanation: A transannular patch disrupts the pulmonic valve, causing chronic PR and progressive RV dilation, the main indication for later pulmonary valve replacement. Residual VSD and RVOT obstruction are less frequent.
exam1.hint: The repair enlarges the RV outflow at the expense of valve competence.

exam1.question: Which combination of features defines tetralogy of Fallot?

options.text: Primum ASD, cleft mitral valve, and inlet VSD
Malaligned VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, and RV hypertrophy
Transposed great arteries with intact septum
Bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, and mitral stenosis

exam1.explanation: Tetralogy consists of an anterior malaligned VSD, an aorta overriding the septum, RVOT obstruction, and RVH. A primum ASD with cleft mitral valve is an AV septal defect.
exam1.hint: Think about the consequences of anterior and superior deviation of the outlet septum.

exam1.question: In Marfan syndrome, aortic root dilation is typically maximal at the

options.text: Distal aortic arch beyond the left subclavian
Aortic annulus only, sparing the sinuses
Sinuses of Valsalva, with effacement of the sinotubular junction

exam1.explanation: Marfan syndrome produces a pear- or flask-shaped root dilated at the sinuses with loss of the sinotubular junction, predisposing to AR and type A dissection. MVP is also common.
exam1.hint: The root loses its normal waist above the sinuses.

exam1.question: According to ASE 2015 chamber quantification, the aortic root at the sinuses of Valsalva is measured

options.text: Inner edge to inner edge at mid-systole
Outer edge to outer edge at end-systole
Trailing edge to leading edge at mid-diastole
Leading edge to leading edge at end-diastole

exam1.explanation: ASE recommends leading edge to leading edge at end-diastole for the aortic root and ascending aorta. In contrast, the aortic annulus is measured inner edge to inner edge in mid-systole.
exam1.hint: The root convention differs from the annulus convention in both edge and timing.

exam1.question: An aortic dissection that involves the ascending aorta is classified as
exam1.explanation: Stanford type A involves the ascending aorta regardless of origin and is a surgical emergency. Type B involves only the aorta distal to the left subclavian artery.
exam1.hint: The Stanford system turns on whether the ascending portion is involved.

exam1.question: In a patient with an acute type A aortic dissection, a new pericardial effusion is concerning because it suggests

options.text: Benign reactive inflammation that needs no action
Rupture of the dissection into the pericardial space

exam1.explanation: Hemopericardium in type A dissection indicates rupture and can rapidly cause tamponade, a leading cause of death. Other complications include acute AR and coronary (usually RCA) involvement.
exam1.hint: Consider where blood goes when the outer aortic wall fails near the root.

exam1.question: A dilated coronary sinus with agitated saline from a left arm vein opacifying the coronary sinus before the right atrium indicates

options.text: Partial anomalous pulmonary venous return to the RA

exam1.explanation: A persistent left SVC usually drains into the coronary sinus, so left-arm contrast enters the coronary sinus first. Right-arm injection would opacify the RA first.
exam1.hint: Track the venous route from the left arm to the heart.

exam1.question: The Nyquist limit in pulsed-wave Doppler equals
exam1.explanation: Aliasing occurs when the Doppler shift exceeds PRF/2. Raising the PRF (by reducing depth) raises the Nyquist limit.
exam1.hint: Sampling must occur at least twice per cycle of the signal.

exam1.question: What is the main limitation of continuous-wave Doppler compared with pulsed-wave Doppler?

options.text: Inability to measure velocities above 2 m/s
Range ambiguity, because velocities along the entire beam are recorded

exam1.explanation: CW Doppler uses separate transmitting and receiving elements so it does not alias, but it cannot localize the depth of the highest velocity. PW Doppler is range-specific but aliases.
exam1.hint: CW sacrifices depth localization to measure very high velocities.

exam1.question: Which adjustment reduces aliasing in pulsed-wave Doppler?
exam1.explanation: A shallower sample volume allows a higher PRF and Nyquist limit, reducing aliasing. Higher transmitted frequencies increase the Doppler shift and worsen aliasing.
exam1.hint: Shorter round-trip travel time permits more pulses per second.

exam1.question: If the Doppler beam is at 60 degrees to the direction of blood flow and no angle correction is applied, the measured velocity will be what fraction of the true velocity?
exam1.explanation: The Doppler shift is proportional to the cosine of the angle, and cos 60 degrees = 0.5, so velocity is underestimated by half. Echo assumes parallel alignment, so poor alignment underestimates gradients.
exam1.hint: Use the cosine of the insonation angle.

exam1.question: Which echo modality offers the highest temporal resolution?
exam1.explanation: M-mode samples a single line very frequently (about 1000-2000 times per second), making it ideal for timing rapid events. 2D, color, and 3D require many scan lines per frame.
exam1.hint: Fewer scan lines per frame allow faster sampling.

exam1.question: Tissue Doppler imaging is configured to display which signals?

options.text: Low-velocity, high-amplitude signals from the myocardium
Low-velocity, low-amplitude signals from the pericardium

exam1.explanation: TDI bypasses the high-pass wall filter and lowers gain to capture the slow, strong myocardial signals. Conventional blood-flow Doppler filters out these signals.
exam1.hint: Myocardium moves slowly but reflects strongly compared with blood.

exam1.question: A recognized drawback of tissue harmonic imaging in echocardiography is that

options.text: Valve leaflets may appear artificially thickened

exam1.explanation: Harmonic imaging improves endocardial definition and reduces near-field clutter, but it can make valves appear thicker than they are. Measure leaflet thickness with fundamental imaging when in doubt.
exam1.hint: Consider how the improved image affects the apparent thickness of thin structures.

exam1.question: When using transpulmonary ultrasound enhancing agents for LV opacification, the system should be set to

options.text: Maximum output power with low gain
A low mechanical index (typically under about 0.3)

exam1.explanation: Low MI imaging preserves microbubbles so the LV cavity opacifies and endocardial borders are defined. High MI destroys bubbles; brief high-MI flash pulses are used only for perfusion replenishment.
exam1.hint: Higher acoustic pressure destroys the microbubbles.

exam1.question: During an agitated saline study, bubbles appear in the left atrium within 3 cardiac cycles of right atrial opacification. This most likely indicates

options.text: An intracardiac right-to-left shunt such as a PFO

exam1.explanation: Early arrival (within about 3 beats) suggests an intracardiac shunt such as a PFO, while late arrival (after about 3-5 beats) suggests intrapulmonary shunting. Saline bubbles do not normally cross the lungs.
exam1.hint: Timing of left heart bubble arrival separates the shunt locations.

exam1.question: Which maneuver increases the sensitivity of an agitated saline study for detecting a patent foramen ovale?

options.text: Injection during a cough-free breath-hold in expiration

exam1.explanation: Valsalva release transiently raises RA pressure above LA pressure, promoting right-to-left flow across a PFO. The RA should be well opacified at the moment of release.
exam1.hint: Transiently reverse the normal interatrial pressure gradient.

exam1.question: Which condition is a contraindication to transesophageal echocardiography?
exam1.explanation: Esophageal pathology such as stricture, tumor, perforation, or recent esophageal surgery contraindicates TEE. Atrial fibrillation and prosthetic valves are common indications.
exam1.hint: The contraindication involves the path the probe must travel.

exam1.question: Which TEE view best displays the superior vena cava, interatrial septum, and inferior vena cava together?

options.text: Midesophageal bicaval view at about 90-110 degrees

exam1.explanation: The ME bicaval view shows the SVC, IAS, and IVC in one plane and is used for sinus venosus ASD, PFO, and catheter assessment. The four-chamber view shows only part of the septum.
exam1.hint: Rotate the multiplane angle toward 90-110 degrees and turn the probe toward the patient's right from the midesophageal level.

exam1.question: Which TEE view is most commonly used to monitor global and regional LV function intraoperatively?

options.text: Upper esophageal aortic arch long-axis view

exam1.explanation: The transgastric mid short-axis view shows all three coronary territories at once and is ideal for monitoring wall motion and filling. The aortic valve and bicaval views do not show the LV myocardium.
exam1.hint: Choose the view showing all three coronary territories in one cross section.

exam1.question: A linear echo within the ascending aorta that moves parallel to a strong reflector and lies at twice its depth most likely represents

options.text: Side-lobe artifact from the aortic valve
Mirror-image artifact of the pulmonary artery

exam1.explanation: Reverberation artifacts appear at multiples of the distance to a strong reflector and move with it, mimicking a dissection flap. A true flap moves independently and separates flow in two lumens on color.
exam1.hint: Measure the distance from the transducer to the strong reflector and compare.

exam1.question: According to the ALARA principle, which adjustment is preferred when the displayed echoes are too dark?

options.text: Increase output power before adjusting gain
Lengthen the scan time to improve detail
Increase receiver gain before increasing output power

exam1.explanation: ALARA favors receiver gain because it amplifies received echoes without increasing patient exposure. Output power raises acoustic exposure.
exam1.hint: Recall which controls affect acoustic exposure to the patient and which only process returning echoes.

exam1.question: Which TEE view, obtained from the midesophagus at about 30-60 degrees, displays all three aortic cusps en face?
exam1.explanation: At roughly 30-60 degrees from the midesophagus, the AV short-axis view shows the three cusps and is used for planimetry and identifying bicuspid valves. The ME long-axis view (about 120-140 degrees) shows two cusps.
exam1.hint: At about 30-60 degrees the imaging plane is perpendicular to the aortic root, whereas about 120-140 degrees cuts it lengthwise.

exam1.question: In a healthy 25-year-old, which phase of diastole contributes the largest share of left ventricular filling?
exam1.explanation: In young healthy hearts, brisk active relaxation creates a suction effect so that roughly 70-80% of LV filling occurs during the early rapid filling phase (mitral E wave). Atrial contraction normally adds only about 15-25%, although its share increases with age and impaired relaxation; no filling occurs during isovolumic relaxation.
exam1.hint: Think about which mitral inflow wave is dominant in a young, compliant ventricle.

exam1.question: A 60-year-old with chronic aortic regurgitation has a blood pressure of 130/60 mmHg. The CW Doppler AR end-diastolic velocity is 3 m/s. What is the estimated LV end-diastolic pressure?
exam1.explanation: The end-diastolic AR gradient is 4 x 3² = 36 mmHg, which equals aortic diastolic pressure minus LVEDP. LVEDP is therefore 60 - 36 = 24 mmHg. Choosing 36 mmHg mistakes the gradient itself for the LV pressure.
exam1.hint: The AR end-diastolic gradient is the difference between aortic diastolic pressure and LV end-diastolic pressure.

exam1.question: A 69-year-old has a calcified aortic valve with a peak velocity of 3.4 m/s, a mean gradient of 26 mmHg, and an AVA of 1.2 cm². LVEF is normal. How should the aortic stenosis be graded?
exam1.explanation: Moderate AS is defined by a peak velocity of 3.0-3.9 m/s, a mean gradient of 20-39 mmHg, and an AVA of 1.0-1.5 cm², and all three parameters agree here. Mild AS has a velocity of 2.0-2.9 m/s and mean gradient under 20 mmHg, and sclerosis implies a velocity of 2.5 m/s or less.
exam1.hint: Check each parameter against the guideline ranges; they are concordant.

exam1.question: A 58-year-old with mitral regurgitation has a stroke volume at the mitral annulus of 120 mL and an LVOT stroke volume of 70 mL, with no aortic regurgitation. What are the regurgitant volume and regurgitant fraction?

options.text: 50 mL and 42%, consistent with moderate MR
50 mL and 71%, consistent with severe MR
70 mL and 58%, consistent with severe MR
50 mL and 29%, consistent with mild MR

exam1.explanation: Regurgitant volume is mitral inflow stroke volume minus LVOT stroke volume (120 - 70 = 50 mL), and regurgitant fraction is 50/120 = 42%. Both fall in the moderate range (30-59 mL and 30-49%); dividing by the LVOT stroke volume instead of the total mitral inflow gives the erroneous 71%.
exam1.hint: The regurgitant fraction is the regurgitant volume divided by the total volume crossing the leaking valve.

exam1.question: A 55-year-old man has a biplane LVEF of 46%. Using ASE 2015 chamber quantification ranges for men, how should LV systolic function be reported?
exam1.explanation: ASE 2015 ranges for men are normal 52-72%, mildly abnormal 41-51%, moderately abnormal 30-40%, and severely abnormal below 30%, so 46% is mildly abnormal. Moderately abnormal would require an EF of 40% or less.
exam1.hint: The normal range for men begins at 52%.

exam1.question: According to the ischemic cascade, which abnormality occurs first after a reduction in coronary blood flow?
exam1.explanation: The ischemic cascade proceeds from perfusion heterogeneity to metabolic changes, diastolic then systolic dysfunction, ECG changes, and finally angina. Wall motion abnormalities appear earlier than ECG changes or symptoms, which is why stress echo is more sensitive than the ECG, but they are not the first event.
exam1.hint: Start with the event closest to the actual reduction in flow.

exam1.question: Two days after coronary bypass surgery, a 67-year-old becomes hypotensive with rising filling pressures. TTE windows are limited and show no circumferential effusion, but a localized echodensity is suspected behind the left atrium. What is the best next step?

options.text: Report that tamponade has been excluded
Perform TEE to look for a localized posterior hematoma compressing the atria

exam1.explanation: After cardiac surgery, tamponade is often caused by a loculated clot that compresses a single chamber, commonly the atria, without a circumferential effusion or classic signs on TTE. TEE images the posterior structures well and is the next step; a nondiagnostic TTE cannot exclude tamponade in an unstable patient.
exam1.hint: Postoperative tamponade can be focal and posterior, beyond what a limited transthoracic window shows.

exam1.question: A 35-year-old with exertional dyspnea has a thin membrane dividing the left atrium, located above (proximal to) the left atrial appendage, with turbulent flow through an opening in the membrane. The mitral leaflets are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam1.explanation: In cor triatriatum sinister, a membrane separates the pulmonary venous chamber from the true LA, and it lies above the LA appendage, so the appendage communicates with the distal chamber. A supravalvular mitral ring lies below the appendage, close to the mitral annulus, and rheumatic MS involves the leaflets themselves.
exam1.hint: The position of the membrane relative to the appendage distinguishes the two membrane lesions.

exam1.question: According to current US labeling for perflutren-based ultrasound enhancing agents, which is a contraindication to their use?

options.text: Known hypersensitivity to perflutren or polyethylene glycol

exam1.explanation: The current contraindication for perflutren agents is known or suspected hypersensitivity to the agent or its components, including polyethylene glycol. Known right-to-left or bidirectional shunts were removed from the contraindication list, and the agents are not renally toxic and are routinely used with stress echo.
exam1.hint: Earlier shunt restrictions were dropped; the remaining contraindication concerns allergy.

exam1.question: During normal quiet inspiration in a healthy adult, the systolic blood pressure typically falls by how much?
exam1.explanation: Inspiration normally causes a small fall in systolic pressure of less than 10 mmHg because of pooling in the pulmonary veins and mild ventricular interdependence. A fall greater than 10 mmHg is pulsus paradoxus, a clinical hallmark of tamponade, so the larger values describe pathologic, not normal, physiology.
exam1.hint: Normal respiratory variation is small; a larger fall is a pathologic sign associated with tamponade.

exam1.question: A 55-year-old with suspected pulmonary hypertension has an early-diastolic peak pulmonic regurgitation velocity of 3 m/s and an estimated RA pressure of 5 mmHg. Using 4V² plus RA pressure, what is the estimated mean pulmonary artery pressure?
exam1.explanation: The early-diastolic PR gradient approximates the mean PA to RV pressure difference: 4 x 3² = 36 mmHg, and adding RA pressure of 5 mmHg gives about 41 mmHg. Answering 36 mmHg forgets to add the RA pressure; PA diastolic pressure is instead estimated from the end-diastolic PR velocity.
exam1.hint: Use the early (peak) PR velocity for the mean pressure and remember the RA pressure term.

exam1.question: According to ACC/AHA guidelines, which Doppler finding defines very severe aortic stenosis?

options.text: Peak velocity of 4 m/s or more, or mean gradient of 40 mmHg or more
Peak velocity of 5 m/s or more, or mean gradient of 60 mmHg or more
Dimensionless index less than 0.50 with a calcified valve
Peak velocity of 3.5 m/s with an AVA under 1.0 cm²

exam1.explanation: Very severe AS is a peak velocity of at least 5 m/s or a mean gradient of at least 60 mmHg, a group with a high event rate even when asymptomatic. A peak velocity of 4 m/s or a mean gradient of 40 mmHg is the threshold for severe, not very severe, AS.
exam1.hint: The answer is one step above the standard severe thresholds.

exam1.question: Per ASE guidelines, which effective regurgitant orifice area indicates severe aortic regurgitation?
exam1.explanation: For aortic regurgitation, an EROA of 0.30 cm² or more (with a regurgitant volume of 60 mL or more and a regurgitant fraction of 50% or more) indicates severe AR. An EROA of 0.10-0.29 cm² falls in the mild-to-moderate range, so 0.20 cm² is not sufficient.
exam1.hint: The AR threshold is lower than the 0.40 cm² threshold used for primary MR.

exam1.question: A 46-year-old woman with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy has palpitations and complete heart block. Echo shows thinning and akinesis of the basal anteroseptum in a pattern that does not follow a coronary distribution. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam1.explanation: Cardiac sarcoidosis characteristically causes thinning or aneurysm of the basal septum, conduction block, and wall motion abnormalities outside a coronary distribution, and hilar adenopathy suggests systemic sarcoid. Chagas disease typically produces an apical aneurysm, and takotsubo affects the mid and apical segments.
exam1.hint: Link the pulmonary finding and conduction disease to an infiltrative granulomatous process.

exam1.question: A 66-year-old with three-vessel coronary disease and chronic stable angina has a resting akinetic anterior wall of normal thickness. Low-dose dobutamine improves its contraction, and after bypass surgery the segment's function recovers over several months. Which term best describes the segment before surgery?
exam1.explanation: Hibernating myocardium is viable tissue with chronically reduced resting flow that downregulates contraction and recovers after revascularization. Stunned myocardium follows a brief episode of ischemia with restored flow and recovers on its own without revascularization, while transmural scar would not show contractile reserve.
exam1.hint: Distinguish chronic reduced flow that needs revascularization from transient dysfunction after flow is restored.

exam1.question: A 54-year-old undergoes pericardiocentesis for a large effusion with tamponade. After drainage the RA pressure remains elevated, and echo now shows a septal bounce with respiratory ventricular interdependence. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam1.explanation: In effusive-constrictive pericarditis, a stiff visceral pericardium continues to constrain filling after the effusion is removed, so RA pressure stays high and constrictive features such as a septal bounce appear. Restrictive cardiomyopathy does not show exaggerated respiratory interdependence, and reaccumulation would show recurrent fluid.
exam1.hint: The constraint persists even after the fluid is gone.

exam1.question: A 70-year-old hypertensive with acute chest pain has smooth, crescentic thickening of the descending aortic wall measuring 9 mm on TEE, with no intimal flap and no color flow within the thickened area. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Classic dissection with a patent false lumen

exam1.explanation: Intramural hematoma appears as smooth, crescentic or circular aortic wall thickening greater than 5 mm without a visible intimal flap or flow, and it is managed as a variant of acute aortic syndrome. A patent false lumen would show flow and a flap, and atheroma is typically irregular and protrudes into the lumen.
exam1.hint: This acute aortic syndrome has blood within the wall but no communication with the lumen.

exam1.question: On TEE, which view provides the best Doppler alignment with the LVOT and aortic valve for measuring transaortic velocity?

options.text: Upper esophageal aortic arch short-axis view

exam1.explanation: From the deep transgastric position the beam is directed up through the LV apex and aligns nearly parallel with LVOT and transaortic flow, similar to an apical window on TTE. The midesophageal aortic valve short-axis view is excellent for planimetry and cusp anatomy but places flow perpendicular to the beam.
exam1.hint: Doppler needs a view that looks along the outflow tract from the apex.

exam1.question: Which muscular ridge in the right ventricle separates the tricuspid inflow portion from the smooth-walled outflow tract (infundibulum)?
exam1.explanation: The crista supraventricularis is a muscular ridge in the RV that divides the trabeculated inflow from the smooth infundibulum leading to the pulmonic valve. The moderator band is a different RV structure that runs from the septum to the anterior papillary muscle near the apex, while the crista terminalis and Eustachian valve are right atrial structures.
exam1.hint: The answer is an RV structure located near the base, between the tricuspid and pulmonic valves.

exam1.question: A 50-year-old with dyspnea has a peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity of 3.5 m/s and an RVOT VTI of 10 cm. What does the TR velocity to RVOT VTI ratio suggest?

options.text: A ratio of 0.035, indicating normal pulmonary vascular resistance
A ratio of 0.35, indicating low cardiac output with normal resistance
A ratio of 2.9, indicating elevated LA pressure
A ratio of 0.35, suggesting PVR greater than 2 Wood units
