exam2.explanation: A dilated, poorly contracting LV with low stroke volume reduces mitral excursion while enlarging the cavity, widening the gap between the E point and the septum; EPSS over about 7 mm correlates with reduced EF. SAM suggests HCM, fluttering suggests AR, and the last option describes rheumatic MS.
exam2.hint: Low forward flow and a large cavity both widen a specific M-mode distance.

exam2.question: A 70-year-old with heart failure has a peak MR velocity of 5.0 m/s and a systolic blood pressure of 110 mmHg without aortic stenosis. What is the estimated LA systolic pressure?
exam2.explanation: The MR gradient (4 x 25 = 100 mmHg) is the LV-to-LA systolic difference; with systolic BP approximating LV systolic pressure, LA pressure is 110 - 100 = 10 mmHg. Aortic stenosis would invalidate this because LV pressure would exceed arterial pressure.
exam2.hint: Systolic blood pressure stands in for LV pressure when there is no outflow obstruction.

exam2.question: On TEE, a 64-year-old with a bileaflet mechanical mitral prosthesis has small, short, symmetric regurgitant jets originating within the sewing ring at the hinge points. INR is therapeutic and gradients are normal. What do these jets represent?

options.text: Normal washing jets of a mechanical valve

exam2.explanation: Bileaflet mechanical valves have built-in small, low-volume closure and leakage backflow within the sewing ring that helps prevent thrombus. Paravalvular leaks originate outside the sewing ring.
exam2.hint: Note the origin of the jets relative to the ring and the normal gradients.

exam2.question: A 32-year-old with Down syndrome has a defect in the lowest portion of the interatrial septum adjacent to the AV valves, with the mitral and tricuspid valves inserting at the same level. Which associated finding is most likely?

options.text: Apical displacement of the septal tricuspid leaflet
Cleft anterior mitral leaflet with mitral regurgitation

exam2.explanation: Primum ASD is a partial AV septal defect with loss of the normal apical offset of the tricuspid valve and a cleft anterior mitral leaflet that often regurgitates. Anomalous pulmonary venous return is linked to sinus venosus defects.
exam2.hint: This defect belongs to the AV canal spectrum.

exam2.question: When evaluating a suspected bicuspid aortic valve in parasternal short axis, why should the valve be assessed in systole rather than diastole?

options.text: Commissures are visible only during isovolumic relaxation
Systolic frames eliminate reverberation from the aortic root
Calcium is detectable only when the cusps are open
A raphe can make a bicuspid valve look trileaflet when closed

exam2.explanation: In diastole a raphe may mimic a third coaptation line, making a bicuspid valve appear trileaflet; the systolic orifice shape (elliptical with two commissures) is diagnostic. A normal trileaflet valve opens in a triangular shape.
exam2.hint: Compare the closed coaptation pattern with the shape of the open orifice.

exam2.question: On TEE before ablation, a 59-year-old has a bulbous, echogenic linear structure between the LA appendage and the left upper pulmonary vein that sometimes casts a shadow. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Normal ridge between the LA appendage and pulmonary vein
Dissection flap in the pulmonary vein

exam2.explanation: This ridge (sometimes called the coumadin or warfarin ridge) is a normal infolding of the atrial wall between the LAA and the left upper pulmonary vein and can appear bulbous; it is a classic thrombus mimic. Thrombus lies within the appendage cavity.
exam2.hint: Its position between two normal structures is characteristic of a fold of atrial wall.

exam2.question: Which cardiac structure is in direct fibrous continuity with the aortic valve, a relationship seen in the parasternal long-axis view?
exam2.explanation: The anterior mitral leaflet is continuous with the aortic root through the aortomitral curtain, so the LVOT is bordered by the septum and this leaflet. The posterior leaflet attaches to the posterior annulus with no aortic continuity.
exam2.hint: Trace the posterior wall of the aortic root downward into the left ventricle.

exam2.question: During treadmill stress echocardiography, a 58-year-old man reaches target heart rate. Post-exercise images show an LV cavity larger than at rest, with new hypokinesis of the anterior wall and apex. How should this be interpreted?

options.text: Ischemic response in the LAD territory

exam2.explanation: A normal response is hyperdynamic wall motion with a smaller end-systolic cavity; new or worsening wall motion abnormalities and cavity dilation indicate ischemia, here in the LAD territory. A fixed scar would be abnormal at rest as well.
exam2.hint: Compare post-exercise cavity size and wall motion with the expected normal response.

exam2.question: A 55-year-old has a circumferential pericardial effusion measuring 2.5 cm in end-diastole. How is the effusion size typically classified?
exam2.explanation: Commonly used cutoffs classify effusions under 1 cm as small, 1-2 cm as moderate, and over 2 cm as large, measured in diastole. Hemodynamic significance depends on the rate of accumulation, not size alone.
exam2.hint: Compare the diastolic depth with the 1 cm and 2 cm cutoffs.

exam2.question: A 61-year-old woman with scleroderma has a peak TR velocity of 3.5 m/s. The IVC measures 2.4 cm and collapses less than 50% with a sniff. What is the estimated RVSP?
exam2.explanation: 4 x 3.5² = 49 mmHg; a dilated IVC (over 2.1 cm) with less than 50% collapse indicates RA pressure of about 15 mmHg, giving RVSP of about 64 mmHg. Adding 3 mmHg (52) or 8 mmHg (57) ignores the IVC findings.
exam2.hint: Add the RA pressure that matches a plethoric, poorly collapsing IVC to 4V².

exam2.question: A sonographer switches to tissue harmonic imaging in a patient with poor windows. What is a recognized pitfall of this mode?

options.text: Valves and thin structures can appear thicker

exam2.explanation: Harmonic imaging improves endocardial definition and reduces near-field and side-lobe artifacts, but it lowers axial resolution, making leaflets look thicker. Caution is needed when judging leaflet thickening.
exam2.hint: Harmonic imaging trades away some axial detail.

exam2.question: During an apical four-chamber view in a 30-year-old woman, a thick muscular band is seen crossing the apical third of the right-sided ventricle from the septum to the free wall. What is the most likely identity of this structure?
exam2.explanation: The moderator band (septomarginal trabecula) is a normal RV muscle band that carries part of the right bundle branch and helps identify the morphologic RV. A Chiari network and Eustachian valve are thin, mobile right atrial remnants, not ventricular muscle.
exam2.hint: It is muscular and lies in the ventricle, not the atrium; consider which normal RV structures can mimic a mass.

exam2.question: Why must post-exercise images be acquired within about 1 minute of stopping a treadmill stress echo?

options.text: Heart rate increases further during early recovery
Ischemic wall motion abnormalities can resolve quickly in recovery
Ultrasound enhancing agents stop working after 1 minute
Acoustic windows always worsen when the patient lies down

exam2.explanation: Exercise-induced wall motion abnormalities may normalize rapidly as heart rate and demand fall, so delayed imaging can miss ischemia (a false negative). Heart rate falls, not rises, after exercise stops.
exam2.hint: Consider what happens to myocardial oxygen demand once exercise ends.

exam2.question: A 29-year-old woman who injects drugs has fever and blood cultures positive for Staphylococcus aureus. Where is a vegetation most likely to be found on echocardiography?

options.text: Ventricular side of the tricuspid leaflets
Aortic side of the aortic cusps
Atrial side of the tricuspid leaflets

exam2.explanation: Injection drug use favors right-sided endocarditis, and vegetations on AV valves typically form on the low-pressure upstream (atrial) side in the path of the regurgitant jet. Semilunar valve vegetations favor the ventricular side.
exam2.hint: Vegetations tend to form on the low-pressure side where a regurgitant jet strikes.

exam2.question: A 66-year-old man with severe COPD and hyperinflated lungs has nondiagnostic parasternal and apical windows. Which acoustic window is most likely to provide adequate images?
exam2.explanation: Hyperinflation flattens the diaphragm, displaces the heart inferiorly, and interposes lung anteriorly, so the subcostal window using the liver is often best. Suprasternal and right parasternal windows are used mainly for the aorta and aortic jets.
exam2.hint: Flattened diaphragms move the heart toward the abdomen, where the liver can transmit sound.

exam2.question: A 32-year-old who had tetralogy of Fallot repair with a transannular patch in childhood has a dilated RV. The CW pulmonic regurgitation signal is dense and ends well before end-diastole, with diastolic flow reversal in the branch pulmonary arteries. What is the most likely finding?
exam2.explanation: Free pulmonic regurgitation after a transannular patch rapidly equalizes PA and RV diastolic pressures, so the dense jet ends early, with branch PA flow reversal; it is the main cause of late RV dilation. A long, gradually decelerating PR signal suggests mild PR.
exam2.hint: Rapid pressure equalization shortens the regurgitant signal.

exam2.question: Five days after a first MI, a 74-year-old woman abruptly loses consciousness with pulseless electrical activity. Bedside echo shows a moderate pericardial effusion with echogenic material and RV diastolic collapse. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: LV free wall rupture with hemopericardium

exam2.explanation: Sudden PEA with an effusion containing echogenic clot and tamponade physiology days after MI is characteristic of free wall rupture. Dressler syndrome occurs weeks later with pericarditis and usually a small serous effusion.
exam2.hint: The effusion contents and abrupt collapse suggest blood entering the pericardium.

exam2.question: A 50-year-old man who grew up in rural Bolivia has right bundle branch block and ventricular arrhythmias. Echo shows a thin-walled apical LV aneurysm and he has normal coronary arteries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Chronic Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) classically causes an LV apical aneurysm and inferolateral wall motion abnormalities with RBBB in patients from endemic Latin American regions. Sarcoidosis more typically thins the basal septum.
exam2.hint: Consider which cardiomyopathy endemic to Latin America classically combines an apical aneurysm, RBBB, and normal coronaries.

exam2.question: A 58-year-old with chronic aortic regurgitation has a CW AR pressure half-time of 180 ms. How should this be interpreted?
exam2.explanation: An AR pressure half-time under 200 ms indicates rapid equalization of aortic and LV diastolic pressures and supports severe AR; more than 500 ms suggests mild AR. Because PHT also shortens with elevated LV diastolic pressure, it is supportive rather than definitive.
exam2.hint: A steeper deceleration slope means aortic and LV diastolic pressures equalize faster.

exam2.question: A 70-year-old woman with a small ascending aorta (2.6 cm at the sinotubular junction) has an aortic valve Doppler mean gradient of 42 mmHg, but catheterization shows a mean gradient of 28 mmHg. Which phenomenon most likely explains the discrepancy?

options.text: Underestimation from a poor Doppler intercept angle
Error in the pressure half-time method

exam2.explanation: Doppler records the gradient at the vena contracta, but downstream some kinetic energy converts back into pressure, which is most pronounced when the ascending aorta is small (under 3.0 cm). Catheterization measures pressure further downstream, so Doppler overestimates the net gradient; angle error would make Doppler read lower, not higher.
exam2.hint: Ask where along the jet each technique measures pressure and how a narrow aorta affects that.

exam2.question: In the parasternal long-axis view, severe aortic regurgitation is indicated when the ratio of jet width to LVOT diameter is at least
exam2.explanation: A central AR jet whose width is 65% or more of the LVOT diameter, measured just below the valve, supports severe AR. A ratio under 25% suggests mild AR, and intermediate values are consistent with moderate AR; eccentric jets make this measurement less reliable.
exam2.hint: Severe AR fills most of the outflow tract width.

exam2.question: In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a maximal LV wall thickness of at least what value is considered a major risk factor for sudden cardiac death?
exam2.explanation: Massive hypertrophy with a maximal wall thickness of 30 mm or more in any segment is an established major risk factor for sudden death in HCM. A thickness of 15 mm is the usual diagnostic threshold, not a risk marker, so accurate measurement of the thickest segment is important.
exam2.hint: The risk marker is 'massive' hypertrophy, far beyond the diagnostic threshold.

exam2.question: In a standard dobutamine stress echocardiography protocol, dobutamine is infused in 3-minute stages starting at 5 mcg/kg/min and increased to a maximum of
exam2.explanation: The typical protocol escalates dobutamine through 5, 10, 20, 30, and 40 mcg/kg/min in 3-minute stages, with atropine added if target heart rate is not reached. Stopping at 20 mcg/kg/min would usually provide inadequate stress, and doses beyond 40 mcg/kg/min are not standard.
exam2.hint: After the low-dose viability stages of 5 and 10 mcg/kg/min, the dose climbs in 10 mcg/kg/min steps over the remaining 3-minute stages.

exam2.question: What is the most common primary malignant cardiac tumor in adults, which typically arises in the right atrium?
exam2.explanation: Angiosarcoma is the most common primary cardiac malignancy in adults and usually arises from the right atrial free wall, often with pericardial involvement. Rhabdomyoma, lipoma, and fibroma are benign tumors, and rhabdomyoma occurs mainly in children with tuberous sclerosis.
exam2.hint: Think of a vascular tumor that favors the right atrial free wall and often involves the pericardium.

exam2.question: A 40-year-old who had mitral valve surgery has a 5 m/s systolic jet entering the right atrium just above the septal tricuspid leaflet. Treating it as TR would give an RVSP over 100 mmHg, yet the RV is normal in size and septal motion is normal. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Left ventricle to right atrium (Gerbode) shunt

exam2.explanation: A Gerbode defect, congenital or after valve surgery or endocarditis, shunts blood from the high-pressure LV into the RA, producing a high-velocity systolic jet that can be mistaken for TR and falsely suggests pulmonary hypertension. A normal RV and septum argue against true severe PH, and a ruptured sinus of Valsalva would cause continuous rather than purely systolic flow.
exam2.hint: The jet velocity reflects the systolic pressure difference between two chambers other than the RV and RA.

exam2.question: While imaging a patient with a rapid heart rate, the sonographer needs a higher 2D frame rate to assess fast wall motion. Which adjustment most effectively increases frame rate?

options.text: Increase the number of focal zones
Narrow the sector width and reduce the imaging depth
Add a large color Doppler box

exam2.explanation: Frame rate rises when each frame needs fewer scan lines (narrower sector) and each line takes less time to listen for echoes (shallower depth). Adding focal zones, increasing line density, or adding color Doppler all increase the time per frame and lower the frame rate.
exam2.hint: Frame rate depends on how many pulses are needed per frame and how long each pulse takes to return.

exam2.question: What is the approximate normal mitral valve orifice area in an adult?
exam2.explanation: The normal adult mitral valve area is about 4 to 6 cm². Symptoms of mitral stenosis generally appear once the area falls below about 2.5 cm², and an area of 1.5 cm² or less is considered severe, so 1.0 to 1.5 cm² describes severe stenosis rather than normal.
exam2.hint: The normal mitral orifice is larger than the normal aortic valve area of 3 to 4 cm².

exam2.question: Why does the Doppler-derived peak gradient across a stenotic aortic valve typically exceed the peak-to-peak gradient reported from cardiac catheterization?

options.text: Doppler angle error systematically overestimates jet velocity
Doppler gives the peak instantaneous gradient, while peak-to-peak compares maxima that occur at different times
Catheters cannot record pressure in the left ventricle
Sedation during catheterization lowers the cardiac output

exam2.explanation: Doppler measures the maximal instantaneous pressure difference, whereas the catheter peak-to-peak gradient subtracts peak aortic from peak LV pressure even though they do not occur simultaneously, so it is smaller. Angle error causes Doppler to underestimate, not overestimate, velocity; mean gradients correlate well between the two methods.
exam2.hint: Consider whether the two peak pressures being compared happen at the same instant.

exam2.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four components of the Wilkins echocardiographic score used to assess suitability for mitral balloon valvotomy?
exam2.explanation: The Wilkins score grades leaflet mobility, leaflet thickening, leaflet calcification, and subvalvular thickening, each from 1 to 4; a total of 8 or less favors balloon valvotomy. Left atrial size is relevant to the clinical picture but is not part of the score.
exam2.hint: All four components describe the valve apparatus itself.

exam2.question: A non-obese 72-year-old with a body surface area of 2.0 m² has an aortic bioprosthesis with an effective orifice area of 1.2 cm² by continuity. Leaflets are thin and move normally. What does this indicate?
exam2.explanation: The indexed EOA is 1.2/2.0 = 0.60 cm²/m², and in a non-obese patient a value of 0.65 cm²/m² or less indicates severe patient-prosthesis mismatch (0.65-0.85 is moderate). Thin, normally moving leaflets argue against structural degeneration; the valve is simply too small for the patient.
exam2.hint: Index the orifice area to body surface area before grading.

exam2.question: Using pulsed tissue Doppler of the lateral tricuspid annulus, an RV index of myocardial performance (RIMP) greater than which value indicates RV dysfunction per ASE?
exam2.explanation: RIMP is (isovolumic contraction time + isovolumic relaxation time) divided by ejection time, and ASE lists a tissue Doppler RIMP above 0.54 (or a pulsed Doppler RIMP above 0.43) as abnormal. Lower values such as 0.35 fall within the normal range.
exam2.hint: RIMP rises as the isovolumic times lengthen relative to ejection time, and the tissue Doppler cutoff is higher than the pulsed Doppler cutoff.

exam2.question: During dobutamine stress echocardiography in a 64-year-old, which finding is an indication to stop the test?

options.text: Heart rate reaching 70% of age-predicted maximum
New wall motion abnormality in two or more contiguous segments
Systolic blood pressure rising to 170 mmHg

exam2.explanation: Endpoints for dobutamine stress include reaching target heart rate (85% of age-predicted maximum), a new or worsening wall motion abnormality in at least two contiguous segments, significant arrhythmia, severe hypertension (systolic above about 220 mmHg), symptomatic hypotension, or intolerable symptoms. Isolated PVCs and a systolic pressure of 170 mmHg are expected responses, and 70% of maximum heart rate is submaximal.
exam2.hint: The test can stop once it has produced a diagnostic positive result.

exam2.question: TEE in a 72-year-old shows several thin, hair-like filamentous strands 2 to 4 mm long arising from the closure line on the ventricular side of the aortic cusps, with no stalk or frond-like head. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Lambl excrescences are thin, filamentous, degenerative strands at the leaflet coaptation line, common in older adults and usually of no clinical significance. A papillary fibroelastoma is larger, with a pedicle and a frond-like head, and vegetations are typically irregular masses accompanied by clinical evidence of infection.
exam2.hint: The finding is tiny, multiple, thread-like, and arises exactly where the cusps meet.

exam2.question: A 22-year-old woman with short stature, a webbed neck, and primary amenorrhea is referred for echocardiography. Which pair of cardiovascular findings is most expected?

options.text: Bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta
Primum ASD and cleft mitral valve
Supravalvular aortic stenosis and branch pulmonary stenosis
Aortic root dilation and mitral valve prolapse

exam2.explanation: Turner syndrome (45,X) is strongly associated with bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, and aortic dilation with a risk of dissection. Primum ASD with a cleft mitral valve is typical of Down syndrome, and supravalvular AS is typical of Williams syndrome.
exam2.hint: Identify the chromosomal syndrome from the physical features first.

exam2.question: On TEE, which part of the thoracic aorta is most difficult to image because the air-filled trachea and left main bronchus lie between it and the esophagus?

options.text: Distal ascending aorta and proximal arch
Aortic root and sinuses of Valsalva
Distal arch near the left subclavian artery

exam2.explanation: The trachea and left main bronchus cross between the esophagus and the distal ascending aorta and proximal arch, creating a TEE blind spot that can hide dissections or plaque there. The aortic root and the descending aorta lie directly adjacent to the esophagus and are well seen, and the distal arch is usually visible from the upper esophagus.
exam2.hint: Think about which airway structures sit in front of the esophagus at the level of the upper mediastinum.

exam2.question: Per ASE 2015 chamber quantification guidelines, a basal RV diameter greater than which value in an RV-focused apical four-chamber view indicates RV dilation?
exam2.explanation: ASE 2015 lists a basal RV diameter above 41 mm (and a mid-cavity diameter above 35 mm) in the RV-focused view as dilated. Values such as 33 mm are within normal limits, and waiting until 50 mm would miss many dilated ventricles.
exam2.hint: The dilation cutoff at the base of the RV-focused view is larger than the mid-cavity cutoff.

exam2.question: A 28-year-old with elfin facies, mild intellectual disability, and infantile hypercalcemia has a systolic murmur. Echo shows an hourglass narrowing of the ascending aorta just above the sinuses of Valsalva with high-velocity flow at that level. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Supravalvular aortic stenosis from Williams syndrome

exam2.explanation: Supravalvular AS produces an hourglass narrowing at the sinotubular junction and is classically linked to Williams syndrome (elastin gene deletion), which also causes elfin facies and hypercalcemia. A subaortic membrane obstructs below the valve, and coarctation is found in the descending aorta near the ductus.
exam2.hint: Locate the obstruction relative to the valve and match it with the syndrome described.

exam2.question: After transcatheter aortic valve replacement, a paravalvular jet is assessed in the short-axis view just below the stent. A circumferential extent of the jet of at least what percentage of the valve perimeter suggests severe paravalvular regurgitation?
exam2.explanation: Per ASE prosthetic valve guidance, a paravalvular jet involving under 10% of the circumference suggests mild, 10-29% moderate, and 30% or more severe regurgitation. A 10% extent is the lower bound of moderate, so it does not by itself indicate severe leak.
exam2.hint: Paravalvular leaks are graded in bands of circumferential extent, with mild leaks involving less than 10%.

exam2.question: A 52-year-old woman receiving doxorubicin had a baseline LVEF of 62%. Follow-up 3D echo shows an LVEF of 45%. How should this be interpreted according to the ASE/EACVI expert consensus?

options.text: Subclinical dysfunction requiring strain confirmation only

exam2.explanation: A decrease in LVEF of more than 10 percentage points to a value below the normal limit (53%) meets the definition of cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction. A 17-point drop is far beyond the variability of 3D echo, and strain is mainly used to detect subclinical changes before EF falls.
exam2.hint: Compare both the size of the drop and the final value with the consensus definition.
